sections.html:
Bothell is a growing Eastside suburb of 52,199 people (July 1, 2025) along the Sammamish River, near the northeast end of Lake Washington. It is a high-value, owner-heavy market: nearly two thirds of households own, and the median home value sits well above $900,000. Sellers can use an agent, go it alone, or take a cash offer.

Housing measureBothell figure
Owner-occupied housing rate, 2020 to 202465.5%
Median value of owner-occupied homes, 2020 to 2024$925,100
Median gross rent, 2020 to 2024$2,346
Households, 2020 to 202419,448
Median household income, 2020 to 2024$140,427

Bothell is one of six Washington cities that span more than one county. The boundary follows Northeast 205th Street, which becomes 244th Street Southwest, and many north-south streets change numbers when they cross it. The city annexed Canyon Park in 1992, and that is how its limits reached into Snohomish County.

Your property tax statement shows which county bills the house. Excise tax is paid to the treasurer of the county where the property sits, so the affidavit and payment go to whichever county holds your parcel. The split also decides which utilities you transfer at closing.

  • Electricity comes from Puget Sound Energy on the King County side and from the Snohomish County Public Utility District on the Snohomish side. Puget Sound Energy supplies natural gas across the whole city.
  • Four water districts serve the city: Alderwood, Bothell, Northshore and Woodinville.
  • The city contracts with Recology for curbside garbage, recycling and yard waste.

Jobs drive demand. The Canyon Park and North Creek business districts have made Bothell a regional employment center, and the city has the second-largest biotechnology hub in Washington, with 61 companies and about 4,000 employees. The University of Washington Bothell and Cascadia College share a campus east of downtown.

A 2022 city study found that among residents who work elsewhere, 29 percent commute to Seattle, 14 percent to Bellevue, 12 percent to Redmond and 8 percent to Kirkland, and 26 percent of residents work from home. Those buyers care about highway access: Interstate 405 meets State Route 522 here, and State Routes 524 and 527 serve the north. Community Transit routes from the Canyon Park hub, including the Swift Green Line, connect Bothell to Lynnwood, Mill Creek and Everett. Average travel time to work is 27.7 minutes.

About 41 percent of Bothell's land is zoned for single-family homes. A listing can name the part of town it belongs to:

  • Downtown Bothell lies north of the Sammamish River between Westhill and Interstate 405.
  • Canyon Park and North Creek are commercial and industrial districts.
  • Maywood and Beckstrom Hill sit north of downtown, east of the Bothell-Everett Highway.
  • Waynita, Simonds and Norway Hill cover the area south of the river and west of the freeway.
  • Brickyard Road and Queensgate occupy the southeast corner.

The Northshore School District serves Bothell, with 35 schools, 12 of them inside the city. Bothell High School, Inglemoor and North Creek high schools all draw Bothell students. Slopes south of the Sammamish River are prone to landslides, and wetlands and creeks run through town, so ask the city whether your lot touches a critical area.

The Permit Center takes permit and land use applications online only, through MyBuildingPermit.com, and answers questions at 425-806-6400 or permits@bothellwa.gov. New zoning rules took effect on January 1, 2025 under BMC 12.14, and the city's CobMap tool shows a parcel's zoning and environmental layers. A buyer planning to add a unit or split a lot should look at that map first.

  • Cutting a tree generally needs no permit on an existing lot under 20,000 square feet with no wetlands, streams, steep slopes over 40 percent or shoreline designation.
  • Construction noise is limited to 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Saturdays.
  • If your home's final inspection was more than 90 days ago, the city may not have the plans on file.

Before you sign a contract, ask the Permit Center whether the house has open permits and whether a rental or accessory unit is allowed on the lot.

The seller owes real estate excise tax. RCW 82.45.060 sets four state bands, from 1.1 percent at the bottom to 3 percent at the top, with current break points at $525,000, $1,525,000 and $3,025,000. The local portion is added, and RCW 82.46.010 lets cities and counties impose local layers of up to 0.25 percent and an additional layer of up to 0.5 percent.

The tax is yours under RCW 82.45.080 and falls due at the time of sale. Under RCW 82.45.100, interest begins after one month and penalties climb to 20 percent at three months. If the deed is never recorded, the buyer can become personally liable for unpaid tax, and the county wants the tax paid before recording. The closing agent can give you the exact total for your parcel.

State law sets the first half of the tax at April 30 and the second half at October 31. Snohomish County mails statements in mid-February and warns that mail processing can run until May 15 or November 15 during heavy volume. It also offers an interest and penalty waiver after a taxpayer dies, plus tax reductions for seniors and disabled owners, which the Assessor's Office at 425-388-3540 can explain. For a King County parcel, call the county's Treasury Operations to confirm the amount before you sell.

Late tax on residential property with four or fewer units carries nine percent annual interest under RCW 84.56.020. Make sure nothing is delinquent before you list.

With a median value above $900,000, carrying costs add up while a house sits, so weigh the routes first.

  • List with an agent and prepare the house for showings.
  • Sell without an agent and handle the disclosure and the paperwork yourself.
  • Request a cash offer from a buyer who takes the house as-is, which fits an inherited property, deferred repairs or a move with a firm deadline.

Collect the last tax statement, utility accounts and any permit records first. Each one shortens the path to a signed contract.

Confirm the county, gather your documents, and agree on a price and date. Escrow then runs title work, checks for open permits or delinquent tax, and prepares the affidavit. You sign, the treasurer of the right county receives the excise tax, and the deed is recorded. With a cash buyer there is no lender appraisal or loan approval to wait for, so timing rests mainly on title and your paperwork.

faqs.q: Which county do I deal with if my Bothell house is near the county line?
faqs.a: The county that bills the property tax on that parcel. Excise tax goes to the treasurer of the county where the property sits, and your tax statement names it.

faqs.q: How is the state excise tax figured on a Bothell sale?
faqs.a: It is a graduated rate, 1.1 percent at the low end up to 3 percent at the top, with local portions added. The closing agent calculates the exact total for your parcel.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Bothell?
faqs.a: April 30 for the first half and October 31 for the second half. State law applies in both King and Snohomish counties.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to cut a tree before I sell my Bothell house?
faqs.a: Usually not on a lot under 20,000 square feet with no wetlands, streams, steep slopes over 40 percent or shoreline designation. Contact a city planner at planning@bothellwa.gov if you are unsure.

faqs.q: Who supplies electricity and water to Bothell homes?
faqs.a: It depends on the side of the county line and the neighborhood. Puget Sound Energy or the Snohomish County PUD supplies power, and one of four water districts supplies water, so confirm both before final readings.
